title: Petrol lawn mower: safe teardown
summary: The prize in a petrol mower is its small four-stroke engine (166 cc and 3.6 kW on Honda's GCV170), with belts, pulleys, axles and bearings as extras. Get the fuel and oil out first, outdoors, and pull the spark plug lead off before you touch the blade.

steps.text: Work outdoors on bare ground or concrete, away from flames, sparks and drains, with an extinguisher or a bucket of sand to hand. No smoking (see safety_fuel_handling).

If the mower has fuel and starts, run it outdoors until it stops by itself, then try to restart it until it won't. That proves the engine runs and empties the tank and carburettor. If it won't run, or you would rather keep the fuel, pump it out into a fuel can with a hand pump (Toro 20333 manual). Then turn the fuel valve off if the mower has one (Honda HRN216 manual).
steps.warn: Never start a siphon by mouth: Toro says never siphon, use a hand pump. Keep hands and feet off the deck while the engine runs: the blade can spin. Never run an engine in a garage or shed: the exhaust holds carbon monoxide, which kills (see safety_carbon_monoxide).

steps.text: Stop the engine and let the engine and muffler cool until you can rest a bare hand on them. Pull the lead off the spark plug and tuck it away so it can't touch the plug. Do this before you go anywhere near the blade (Toro 20333 manual, Honda HRN216 manual).
steps.warn: Turning the blade turns the engine. With the lead on, it can fire and the blade can kick.

steps.text: Electric-start mowers: take off the battery cover and unplug the battery connector before you go further (Honda HRN216 manual). Don't let the battery's terminals touch metal. If it is swollen or leaking, see safety_swollen_lithium or safety_lead_acid.

Drain the oil while it is warm, not hot, and only once the muffler is cool enough to touch: warm oil runs out faster. On the Honda and Toro it comes out of the filler neck. Take out the dipstick, put a container beside the mower and tip the mower on its side, air filter and carburettor side up. Which side differs between makes: Honda says right side, fuel cap up; Toro says air filter up (Honda HRN216 manual, Toro 20333 manual).
steps.warn: Tipping the wrong way lets fuel or oil flood the carburettor and air filter, and fuel leaks from a tank that still holds fuel. Empty the tank first (Toro) and keep the air filter and carburettor side up (Honda: fuel cap side up).

steps.text: Put the used oil in a sealed, labelled container. Don't pour it on the ground or down a drain; one oil change can foul a lot of water (Honda HRN216 manual, EPA used oil).

Remove the blade. Check again that the spark plug lead is off. Wear thick leather gloves and eye protection. With the mower on its side, air filter up, hold the blade with your gloved hand or wedge a block of wood between the blade and the deck, then undo the blade bolts or nuts. The Honda uses a 14 mm socket (Honda HRN216 manual).
steps.warn: The blade is sharp and its bolts are tight (49–59 N·m on the Honda). Brace yourself so your hand can't slide onto the edge when the bolt breaks free.

steps.text: Take off what sits under the blade: the blade adapter or driver, and on mowers with a blade brake the brake disc and its shield. Note the order they stack in. The Toro's parts list shows a small belt, a pulley and three ball bearings in its engine and blade assembly (Toro 20333 parts).
Unhook the control cables at the engine: the blade control or brake cable, the throttle if fitted, and the drive cable on self-propelled mowers. Cut cable ties rather than kinking the cables.
Self-propelled mowers: slip the drive belt off the engine pulley, then unbolt the transmission and the rear axle with its wheels.
Undo the bolts that hold the engine to the deck (the number and position vary by model) and lift the engine off with its fuel tank. A Honda GCV170 weighs about 10 kg (22 lb) dry (Honda GCV170).
steps.warn: The muffler stays hot long after the engine stops. Lift with your legs, not your back. Keep the engine upright: the carburettor can still hold a little fuel.

steps.text: Take the wheels off and pull the axles. Keep the wheel bolts, any bearings and the springs.

Store the engine upright under cover. For long storage, take out the spark plug, pour about 30 ml (1 fl oz) of engine oil into the cylinder, pull the starter cord slowly a few times, and refit the plug loosely (Toro 20333 manual). The crankcase is empty after step 5: refill it to the dipstick mark before you run the engine (Honda HRN216 manual).

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **The engine.** Honda's GCV170 is an air-cooled four-stroke single with overhead valves: 166 cc, making 3.6 kW (4.8 hp) at 3,600 rpm and 11.1 N·m at 2,500 rpm (Honda GCV170). On the HRN216 its maximum governed speed is 2,950–3,100 rpm (Honda HRN216 manual). The crankshaft points straight down, with the blade bolted to its lower end, so whatever it drives has to take power from a downward shaft: a pulley and belt to a pump, a generator head or an alternator (see teardown_car_alternator), mounted with the engine the same way up. Don't adjust the governor to make it run faster: Honda warns the blades could break apart (Honda HRN216 manual). Run it only outdoors; the exhaust holds carbon monoxide (Honda HRN216 manual; see safety_carbon_monoxide).
- **Belts and pulleys.** Self-propelled mowers have a V-belt from the engine to the transmission; mowers with a blade brake have a small belt and pulley under the blade (Toro 20333 parts). Use them for any small belt drive.
- **Transmission and axles.** A small gearbox driving the rear wheels: the Toro 20333 has transmission 115-4652 (Toro 20333 parts); the Honda HRN216 has a variable-speed one giving 0–1.84 m/s (0–4.11 mph) ground speed (Honda HRN216 manual). Axles make shafts for carts and wheelbarrows.
- **Bearings.** The Toro 20333 lists three ball bearings in its engine and blade assembly and two in its transmission and rear drive (Toro 20333 parts).
- **Control cables.** Steel inner cables in sleeves: the Toro parts list has a traction cable and a brake cable; the Honda has a blade control cable and a Smart Drive cable (Toro 20333 parts, Honda HRN216 manual). Reuse for any pull control.
- **Springs.** Torsion springs, and the blade-brake tension spring (Toro 20333 parts, Troy-Bilt TB110 parts).
- **Electric-start parts.** The Honda HRN216 VLA has self-charging electric start, a battery, and a 30 A and a 3 A fuse (Honda HRN216 manual). Charging systems on small engines can use a stator with a diode or a regulator (Briggs charging test). Keep the battery with a 12 V charger (Honda HRN216 manual) and read its label for the chemistry before charging it.
- **Spark plug.** Note its type and gap before you lose the manual: the GCV170 takes an NGK BPR5ES gapped 0.7–0.8 mm (Honda HRN216 manual).

## Variations

- **Honda HRN216 VLA:** GCV170 engine, Smart Drive self-propel, electric start, an upper and a lower blade on two bolts, 0.91 L fuel tank, 0.40 L of SAE 10W-30. Tip it on its right side, fuel cap side up. 39.6 kg (87.3 lb) with grass bag (Honda HRN216 manual).
- **Toro 20333 Recycler:** Briggs & Stratton engine 128M02-0001-F1, self-propelled through a V-belt and transmission, a blade-brake clutch with its own belt and pulley, 0.44 L of SAE 30 or 10W-30. Tip it with the air filter up and the dipstick down. 40 kg (89 lb) (Toro 20333 manual, Toro 20333 parts).
- **Troy-Bilt TB110:** a push mower. Its parts list shows a mulching blade on an adapter, front and rear axle assemblies, torsion springs and one control cable (Troy-Bilt TB110 parts).
- Engine makes differ: read the engine's own label for its model and type before matching parts.

## What to leave

- The recoil starter's inside. Leave it on the engine and closed: its flat spring is wound tight and you need it to start the engine.
- An engine with a bent crankshaft. If the mower shook badly after hitting something, the shaft may be bent (Honda HRN216 manual); that engine will vibrate.
- Stale fuel. Don't pour it on the ground or into drains; label it and see safety_fuel_handling for how to judge it.
- The plastic shrouds and grass bag, unless you need them.

## Testing what you got out

- **The engine:** step 2 is the test. If it ran, it runs. If it didn't, check for fresh fuel, a clean air filter, and a clean, correctly gapped spark plug before giving up on it.
- **Belts:** look for cracks and glazing. A cracked belt will fail under load.
